title: 7 Things Senior PMs Do Instead of "Real" Work
author: The Effective Project Manager
summary: This piece answers a specific and common anxiety among senior project managers: the feeling that as their careers advance, they produce less tangible, visible output. Its argument is that seven largely invisible activities — talking, strategising, unblocking, teaching, thinking, listening, and stressing — constitute the real work of seniority, even though none of them generates the artifacts (documents, spreadsheets, shipped features) that people instinctively recognize as productivity. For each of the seven, the author supplies a specific mechanism for why it counts as work and a concrete practice for improving at it, such as asking 'what's the part of this project you're avoiding?' to surface the information status updates hide. The essay's closing reframe is that seniority is not a matter of doing less real work but of shifting from being the one who does the work to being the reason the work gets done by others at all.
points: The author argues the most important project information almost never appears in status updates and must be drawn out by asking questions that cannot be answered with 'fine' or 'good.'
Strategising is redefined as deciding what a team will not do, tested by asking 'what happens if we do nothing here?' for every item under consideration.
Teaching is framed as a scaling mechanism: solving a problem yourself fixes it once, while teaching someone else to solve it fixes every future recurrence without further involvement.
Listening is distinguished from hearing an update by attention to what is omitted — a slight hesitation or a status that is 'a little too clean' — as an early warning signal.
A senior person's invisible role of absorbing risk and stress ('what if this goes wrong') is presented as a specific, namable form of labor that keeps a team moving quickly and calmly.
quotes: The more senior I get, the less "real" work I seem to do. But I spend more time talking, strategising, unblocking, teaching, thinking, listening, stressing.
The most important project information almost never shows up in a status update. People give you the real info when they trust you enough to say "actually, this isn't going well.
Every hour your team spends on the wrong priority is an hour they don't get back. Picking the right priority, before anyone starts building, is what keeps that from happening.
When you solve a problem yourself, it's fixed once. When you teach someone else how to solve it, it's fixed every time it happens again, without you.
Problems show up first as a slight hesitation, a status that's a little too clean, a person who's gone quiet in meetings. Catching that early is what stops a small issue from becoming a big one.
Nobody warns you about this shift. You stop being the one who does the work. You become the reason the work gets done at all.
